title: Unified SBOM + Driver Compatibility Matrix for LTS Upgrade Orchestration
creator: Ava Patel
description:
Problem: Upgrading runtime and infra stacks across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments is risky because we lack a single source of truth that ties container images to signed SBOMs and a verified CUDA/driver compatibility matrix per LTS channel. This makes canary rollouts and automated gating brittle: operators cannot easily determine whether a given image is safe for a cluster tier, and incident rollback requires manual artifact correlation.

Goal: Produce an automated pipeline and metadata model that: (1) generates and signs SBOMs for every release image; (2) computes and stores a compatibility matrix that pins CUDA/kernel/driver versions to each supported LTS channel and model runtime build; (3) exposes these artifacts to the release orchestration service so rollout gates can automatically allow/deny upgrades based on compatibility, security attestation, and passing test suites.

Scope: CI pipeline changes (image build -> SBOM generation -> attestation), an artifacts metadata store (immutable mapping image tag -> SBOM hash -> driver pinset), integration points with rollout-engine (canary/gate checks), console UI surface for viewing compatibility, and updated runbook for Dedicated/Private upgrade procedures.
acceptance_criteria: Every official container image produced by the build pipeline has a signed SBOM uploaded to the artifact store and linked from the image metadata
A machine-readable driver/CUDA/kernel compatibility matrix exists for each LTS channel and is versioned alongside runtime releases
Rollout orchestration enforces a gate that validates image SBOM signature and compatibility against cluster LTS pinset before progressing beyond canary
CI jobs run the certified compatibility test matrix (GPU smoke tests + KV cache regression) and results are attached to the image metadata
Documentation (Runbook + Console help) describes how to interpret SBOMs, driver pins, and how to request exceptions
Security review completed and artifact signing uses KMS-backed keys; SBOM attestation visible in Console
tasks: Pipeline: add sbom generation step to releases/build-image (owned by eng-ci) - PR: github.com/redwood/release-pipeline/pull/417
Artifact store: design schema for image -> sbom_hash -> driver_matrix (owned by eng-release-infra)
Compatibility ingestion: script to run GPU compatibility matrix and produce pinset JSON per LTS channel
Rollout integration: add gating check to rollout-engine service to query artifact store and enforce compatibility
Console: surface compatibility matrix and SBOM link on image detail page (design review required)
E2E tests: add CI job matrix that runs 3 representative CUDA/driver combos for each LTS channel
progress_updates: 2026-02-26: Spike completed — validated oss-sbom-generator works with our multi-stage build and produces SPDX and CycloneDX outputs. Prototype SBOM uploaded to staging registry.

2026-03-02: Design review with Console and Release teams. Sofia Martinez (Design) approved UX for image detail view + a compact attestation banner. Action: eng-console to implement UI after API contract finalized.
2026-03-05: Draft artifact-store schema posted to docs (confluence: /release-infra/artifacts-metadata). Feedback from security: require KMS-signed SBOMs and tamper-evident storage.

2026-03-08: First compatibility ingestion run completed on a small set of 1.18 and 1.20 runtime images. Identified one incompatible driver version for 1.20 that requires a patch — created ENG-9075 to track the runtime patch.

2026-03-10: Rollout-engine gating prototype implemented in staging; successfully blocked a synthetic upgrade where SBOM signature was removed. Next: add compatibility check and CI attachment ingestion.
notes: We should avoid coupling driver pinsets to a single NVIDIA driver version number; instead store validated combinations (CUDA minor -> driver hash -> kernel minimum). This makes future backports and micro-updates easier.
For Private deployments where customers manage kernels, the gate should emit an explicit 'requires-driver' advisory so operators can reconcile manually.
Long-lived LTS channels require a policy for occasional re-verification (quarterly) and a mechanism to mark a pinset as deprecated if security issues are found.
